samples.text:
Dear Sir or Madam,

Urgent repairs needed at Ming Tak Road Playground

I am writing as a resident of Pak Ling Estate to report several hazards at Ming Tak Road Playground and to ask your office to arrange repairs urgently.

The most serious problem is the swing set. One chain on the left-hand seat has snapped, so the seat now dangles from a single chain and could easily swing into a child's face. Residents have tied red tape around it, but toddlers simply duck underneath. The bottom edge of the slide is also cracked, leaving a sharp piece of plastic exactly where children land, and the rubber mat under the climbing frame has a hole about 30 cm wide. A child tripped there on 28 October. Finally, the lamp by the entrance has not worked since mid-October, so the playground is almost dark after 6:30 pm.

These faults affect many families. The kindergarten next door brings around twenty young pupils here every weekday morning, and families like mine have no safe alternative, as the nearest playground is fifteen minutes away across a busy road. I reported the problems by phone on 20 October, but they remain unresolved.

I would therefore ask you to temporarily fence off the swings, the slide and the climbing frame and to repair the lamp at once. In the longer term, I hope the damaged equipment and mat can be replaced and the playground given routine safety inspections.

Thank you for your attention. I look forward to your reply.

Yours faithfully,
Chris Wong

commentary.content: All three points are covered fully. Each fault from the map is used selectively and its specific danger explained (the seat swinging into a face, plastic where children land); effects on families cite the kindergarten group, the distant alternative and the unanswered report; requests are split clearly into immediate action (fencing off all three dangerous items and repairing the lamp) and longer-term action.
commentary.language: Accurate and varied, with precise vocabulary for the faults (snapped, dangles, cracked, unresolved) and a consistently polite, firm tone. A few sentences are long and list-like, which keeps Language at 6 rather than 7.
commentary.organisation: Purpose is stated at once and a subject line orients the reader; paragraphs move logically from problems to effects to requests; correct formal salutation and close.

samples.text:
Dear Editor,

I am writing in response to the letter "Let Children Play, Not Count" (12 November), in which a parent argued that inter-school matches for students under 15 should stop keeping scores. As a Form 5 student who has played in my school's basketball team since Form 1, I understand the writer's worry, but I strongly disagree with the proposal.

First, removing the score would not remove the pressure; it would only hide it. Players, spectators and coaches always know who is winning. When I was thirteen, our coach arranged a friendly match with no scoreboard, and within ten minutes both benches were counting baskets out loud. The genuine source of stress is not the number on the board but the way adults react to it. If coaches and parents shout at children for losing, they will do so whether or not the score is official.

Second, a score teaches young players lessons that cannot be learned in training. Losing 18–42 to a stronger opponent in my first season was humiliating, but it showed us exactly how far behind we were and gave us the motivation to practise our defence every lunchtime. A year later we lost to the same school by only four points, and that small number did more for our morale than any trophy. Without scores, progress becomes invisible, and so does the satisfaction of improving.

Third, matches without results would be unfair to students who have worked hard. Many young athletes give up their weekends and time with friends to train. Recording the score is one way of respecting that commitment. It is also how coaches identify talented players and how schools decide which teams need extra resources.

That said, the writer is right that some school sport has become too intense. Instead of abolishing scores, schools could limit junior teams to three training sessions a week, ensure every squad member gets playing time, and present awards for teamwork and sportsmanship as well as for winning. After each fixture, coaches could focus on what went well rather than only on the result.

Removing scores would solve the wrong problem. Competition is not the enemy of fun; for many of us, it is part of the fun. Rather than taking the score away from young players, let us teach them how to win and lose well.

Yours faithfully,
Chris Wong

commentary.content: A firm, consistent stance with three well-developed reasons, each grounded in convincing school-sport experience (the match with no scoreboard, the 18–42 defeat and the later four-point loss). The writer engages directly with the parent's concern and offers practical alternatives, showing a strong sense of newspaper readers.
commentary.language: Wide range of accurate structures, including conditionals and balanced sentences; precise topic vocabulary (squad, fixture, sportsmanship, morale) used naturally; confident but courteous tone throughout.
commentary.organisation: Clear introduction linking to the parent's letter, logically ordered arguments and a well-placed concession. First / Second / Third signposting is slightly predictable, so Organisation is 6.

samples.text:
Dear Editor,

I am writing to response the letter which suggest that matches for students under 15 should not keep scores at all. I disagree this suggestion and I have three reasons.

Firstly, keeping scores can make students work harder. When there is a score, students know they need to win, so they will train more hard. For example, our school football team lost in a match last year. After that, all of us practise every Saturday and we won the next match. If there is no score, students will not have the motivation to improve themselves.

Secondly, sports competition is a good chance for students to learn how to face failure. In the real life, we cannot always win. Due to it can teach students to accept losing, the scores are important. If teenagers never lose in a match, they will become very weak when they face difficulties in the future, for example in the public exam or in their work.

Moreover, without scores the matches will become boring. Students and audiences are interested to watch a match because they want to know who will win. If nobody count the scores, the players will not try their best and they will just play for fun. Then the competition is meaningless. Furthermore, some students want to join a sports team in university or become a professional athlete. They need the results to prove their ability.

However, I agree that some coaches are too strict with the students. Some students are very stressful because they train every day and their coach scold them when they lose. The school should talk to the coaches and tell them to be more patient.

In conclusion, I strongly believe that the scores should be kept in inter-school matches. It can let students work harder, learn to face failure and make the matches more interesting. I hope the parents can understand that winning and losing is a part of sports.

Yours faithfully,
Chris Wong

commentary.content: The stance is clear and three relevant reasons are given, with one personal example (the football team training on Saturdays). Development is uneven: the second reason jumps to the public exam and work, and the third partly overlaps the first. The parent's worry about pressure is touched on only at the end and is not answered directly.
commentary.language: Simple sentences are mostly accurate, but there are regular errors in verb forms and typical local patterns (I disagree this suggestion; Due to it can teach; interested to watch; very stressful). Meaning remains clear and the register is suitable.
commentary.organisation: Conventional letter structure with introduction, body and conclusion, but cohesion relies heavily on Firstly / Secondly / Moreover / Furthermore, and the conclusion simply repeats the reasons. Announcing 'three reasons' in the opening is mechanical.

samples.text:
Good afternoon, Mr Lau, teachers and fellow students,

My name is Chris Wong from 5C, and I am standing for president of the Student Union. I am not going to promise you free lunches or a swimming pool on the roof. What I can pledge are three changes that are realistic enough to achieve this year. Over the past two years, as treasurer of the Science Society, I have learned that a proposal only succeeds when someone is willing to do the dull work behind it: booking rooms, chasing replies and persuading teachers. That is the work I am offering to do, and my campaign has three clear objectives.

First, I want to consult the students who never attend Student Union meetings. Last year only about thirty people attended our open meetings, and most of them were already committee members. That is not because the rest of you are indifferent. It is because a meeting in Room 304 at 4:15 on a Friday is not where most of us want to be. If I am elected, every class will answer a two-minute online poll at the start of each month, and the results will be posted on the noticeboard outside the tuck shop. You will see what your classmates think, and so will the principal, which makes our requests far harder to ignore.

Second, I want to turn the library into a place we actually use. At the moment it closes at five, an inconvenient time, just when many of us finish our activities and need somewhere quiet to revise. I have already spoken to Ms Ho, our librarian, and she is willing to stay open until six on two weekdays if students help with the duty. My team will organise a rota of volunteers, and helpers will receive service hours in return.

Third, I want school events to be genuine celebrations that belong to everyone, not only to the sports teams and the prefects. This year's Christmas fair raised money for a worthwhile charity, but how many of you had a say in what was sold or who performed? Under my Union, any club or class will be able to apply for a stall or a five-minute performance slot, and half of them will be kept for juniors.

Some of you may be thinking: we have heard promises like this before. You are right to be sceptical. That is why, for the sake of transparency, I will publish a monthly update showing what we have done and what we have not. If a plan fails, I will acknowledge it openly rather than hide it.

A Student Union is not a club for a few popular students. It is supposed to represent you. Give me your vote next Friday, and give me the chance to prove it.

Thank you.

commentary.content: Three specific, realistic proposals, each explained with concrete details of school life (meetings at 4:15 on a Friday, the library closing at five, the Christmas fair) and each showing how it would work. Credibility is built through relevant experience and a promise of monthly updates, and the speaker anticipates students' scepticism.
commentary.language: Accurate and varied, with effective spoken features: direct address, a rhetorical question, short punchy sentences and a humorous opening. Occasionally the sentences are long for a speech, which keeps Language at 6.
commentary.organisation: Engaging opening, clearly signposted proposals, a well-handled answer to doubters and a memorable closing appeal. The structure suits a spoken campaign speech.

I am Chris Wong from 5C. I am very happy to stand here today. I am the candidate of the Student Union president. Today I want to tell you what I will do if I become the president and why you should vote for me.

First of all, I want to improve the canteen food. Many students complain that the food in our canteen is not delicious and very expensive. Secondly, I want to hold more activities for students. Nowadays students are very stress because of the homework and tests. So I will organise a sports day for every class and a music day during lunch time. Students can relax and make more friends from different forms. Besides, I will invite some famous people to give talks in the hall, so students can learn more things outside the textbook. I believe this activities can make our school life more colourful.

Thirdly, I will let students to have more chance to give their opinions. I will put a suggestion box outside the general office. Every students can write down their ideas and put it inside the box. The Student Union will read all the suggestions every week.

Why you should vote for me? Because I have a lot of experience. I was the class monitor for three years and I am also a member of the basketball team. commentary.organisation: Clear structure with an introduction and paragraphs signposted by First of all / Secondly / Thirdly, but the linking is mechanical and the appeal for votes is tagged on at the end. The rhetorical question is an attempt at a spoken feature.

samples.text:
Selling Before the Bell

Last term, my classmate Ka Yan sold over two hundred hand-painted phone cases from her bedroom. Another friend gives Saturday chess lessons to three primary pupils in his estate. Neither is getting rich, but both have discovered what many Hong Kong teenagers are now trying: being your own boss before leaving school. So is running a small business while you are still a student a smart move or a risky distraction? The honest answer is that it can be both.

What you gain
The most obvious benefit is money, but the real lesson is what money costs. When you have to buy the paint, pay the delivery fee and still charge a price people will accept, you quickly learn the difference between income and profit. Ka Yan's first batch of cases actually lost her forty dollars, because she forgot to include the cost of packaging. It is a mistake she has not made again.

A business also teaches skills that no textbook can. Replying politely to an angry customer at eleven at night, keeping accurate records of orders, or explaining a chess opening to an impatient nine-year-old all build confidence and resilience. These are exactly the qualities universities and employers say they want, and a student seller can point to real evidence of them.

What you risk
However, every hour spent on orders is an hour not spent on revision or sleep. Most of us already have long school days, tutorial classes and piles of homework, and a business that keeps growing can quietly swallow your evenings. Several student entrepreneurs I know admitted that their marks slipped in the very term their shops became popular.

There are also dangers that are easy to overlook. Online buyers sometimes refuse to pay, or ask to meet in person, and a teenager arranging to meet a stranger outside an MTR station alone is taking a genuine risk. Some schools also have rules about selling goods on campus, and parents who pay you for lessons will expect you to turn up even during exam weeks.

Making it work
None of this means you should abandon a good idea. Before you start, consult your parents, limit the hours you spend on it each week, and agree that it pauses during exams. Insist on secure payment methods, never meet buyers on your own, and keep your goals modest. The aim is not to become a tycoon by Form 6, but to learn how the real world works while the stakes are still small.

Run carefully, a small business can be one of the most useful lessons of your school life. Run carelessly, it can cost you far more than you earn.

commentary.content: Both benefits and risks are discussed in depth with specific, believable examples from Hong Kong student life (the phone cases that first lost forty dollars, the chess lessons, meeting a buyer outside an MTR station). The writer weighs the two sides sensibly and ends with practical advice, showing a strong sense of teenage magazine readers.
commentary.language: Accurate and varied, with precise vocabulary for money and business (income and profit, batch, packaging, stakes) and a lively, direct tone. A few sentences are long and list-like, so Language is 6 rather than 7.
commentary.organisation: An engaging opening built on two classmates' examples, purposeful subheadings that separate gains, risks and advice, smooth transitions and a balanced closing line that answers the question in the title.

samples.text:
Students Doing Business: Good or Bad?

Nowadays, many secondary students in Hong Kong start their own small business. Some of them sell handmade accessories on the internet, some of them teach younger children to play piano. In this article, I will discuss the benefits and risks of running a small business as a student.

Firstly, running a business can let students to earn their own pocket money. My cousin is a Form 4 student and she sells handmade bookmarks online. Every month she can earn about five hundred dollars. She does not need to ask money from her parents, so she feel more independent. She also learn how to save money and how to decide the price.

Secondly, students can learn many useful skills. For example, they need to communicate with customers and solve problems when something goes wrong. These skills are very important for their future career. Moreover, it can make students more confident, because they know they can do something by themselves.

On the other hand, running a small business also have some risks. The biggest risk is students will spend too much time on it. Hong Kong students already have a lot of homework and tests. If they need to reply the customers every night, they will not have enough time to study and sleep. My cousin's result drop a little last term because she was too busy with her orders.

Another risk is about safety. Some buyers on the internet are not honest. They may not pay the money, or they may ask to meet the student alone in a quiet place. It is very dangerous for teenagers. Also, students may lose money if nobody buy their products.

In conclusion, running a small business as a student have both benefits and risks. I think students can try it, but they must balance their study and their business. Parents should also give advice to them. If students can manage their time well, it will be a valuable experience.

commentary.content: Both benefits and risks are covered with relevant points and one personal example (the cousin who sells bookmarks), so the task is met. However, the other examples are general, the skills paragraph is thin, and the ending gives general instructions rather than practical advice for readers.
commentary.language: Communication is clear, but errors in agreement, verb patterns and prepositions are frequent (can let students to earn; she feel more independent; reply the customers; running a small business also have some risks), and the opening has a comma splice. Vocabulary is adequate but plain and often repeated.
commentary.organisation: Clear paragraphs in a predictable order (introduction – benefits – risks – conclusion), but cohesion relies on Firstly / Secondly / Moreover / On the other hand, and the opening 'In this article, I will discuss' and the 'In conclusion' ending read like an essay rather than a magazine article.

Nowadays many student in Hong Kong have small business. For example sell things online or teach the children. Some of my classmate also do it. I think it is a good things.

samples.text:
The notebook had been left on the back seat of the minibus, and nobody else seemed to have noticed it. It was small and brown, its cover so worn and wrinkled that it felt like cloth. I told myself I would hand it to the driver at the terminus. Instead, somewhere between the third and fourth stops, curiosity won and I opened it.

There were no names inside, nothing to identify the owner, only drawings. Page after page of pencil sketches: a schoolboy asleep against the fogged window, his tie twisted; a weary woman in a cleaner's uniform counting coins; a man clutching a birthday cake on his knees as if it were fragile glass. Under each drawing was a single anonymous line in small, neat handwriting. "Hope the exam went well." "You deserve a seat." "I hope she likes it."

I recognised the seats, the yellow handrail, the faded sticker on the window. Every one of these commuters had ridden this minibus. Then, near the end, I stopped abruptly.

It was my brother. Kit was hunched in the corner seat in his muddy football kit, his face pressed against the window. I remembered the day vividly: the afternoon his team lost the final and he cried silently all the way home. I had been sitting right beside him, but the artist had left me out. Underneath, the line read, "Tomorrow will be lighter."

I did not hand the notebook to the driver. For the next week I sat in the back row every afternoon, holding it on my lap and studying every passenger who boarded. On Thursday, an old man with a walking stick climbed in, glanced at the notebook, then at me, and smiled with a peculiar certainty, as if we had already been introduced.

His name was Mr Fung. He had taught art for thirty-five years, he said, and since his wife's death he had ridden the same route most afternoons, because grief was easier to carry in a crowd than in an empty flat. A cold had kept him at home for several days. "People on minibuses are honest," he told me. "They think nobody is watching." He had given the notebook up for lost.

Before his stop, I hesitated, then handed it back, overwhelmed by a sudden impulse to thank him. He turned to Kit's page, took out a pencil and drew for a minute before passing it to me again. Next to the crying boy, there was now a second sketch: the same boy in the back seat, grinning, with a football on his knees. That evening, Kit saw it and laughed for the first time in a week.

I have my own sketchbook now. My portraits are terrible, but whenever I take the minibus, I look for someone who needs a kind line written underneath.

commentary.content: An original, moving plot in which the notebook's contents drive every event: the sketches, the narrator finding her brother's portrait, the search, and the meeting with Mr Fung. Characters have clear motives, there is a strong turning point, and the ending, in which the new sketch reaches the brother, resolves the story while echoing the opening.
commentary.language: Controlled past and past perfect tenses, varied sentence lengths used for effect, precise description (fogged window, clutching a birthday cake, fragile glass) and accurately punctuated dialogue. Vocabulary is apt without being showy.
commentary.organisation: Well-paced paragraphs build towards the discovery and the meeting; time shifts are handled smoothly, and the final paragraph links back to the notebook and the minibus.

samples.text:
The notebook had been left on the back seat of the minibus, and nobody else seemed to have noticed it. I was very curious, so I picked it up and open it. Inside the notebook, there were many notes about Chemistry and some drawings. On the first page, there was a name: Marcus Tse, 6B, Kwun Hill College.

I felt very worry because the public exam was coming and the notes looked very important. If I am Marcus, I will be very upset if I lost my notes. So I decided to return the notebook to him. However, I did not know where is Kwun Hill College. I searched on the internet and found that it was near to my school.

Next day, I went to Kwun Hill College after school. The security guard stopped me and asked me what I wanted. I explained him the whole story, but he said he cannot let me go inside. I was very disappointed. Suddenly, a tall boy walked out of the school gate. He looked very worried and he was checking his bag again and again. I thought he may be Marcus, I asked him, "Are you Marcus Tse?" He was surprised and said yes.

When I gave the notebook to him, he was so happy that he almost cried. He told me that he spent two years to write those notes and he could not study without them. He said thank you to me many times and he invited me to have a milk tea in a cafe near his school.

After that day, we became good friends. We study together in the library every weekends and he taught me Chemistry. Finally, both of us got good results in the exam.

From this experience, I learnt that helping others is a happy thing. If we help other people, other people will help us too. I will always remember this special day.

commentary.content: A coherent plot that grows from the notebook and includes a small complication (the security guard), but it is predictable, description is limited, and the ending is rushed (both got good results) and followed by a stated moral.
commentary.language: Past tense is mostly maintained, but there are regular slips in conditionals, reported speech and verb forms (If I am Marcus, I will be very upset; he said he cannot let me; spent two years to write). Vocabulary is simple but adequate.
commentary.organisation: Clear chronological paragraphs with simple time connectives (Next day, Suddenly, After that day, Finally). The moral paragraph at the end weakens the shape of the story.

The notebook had been left on the back seat of the minibus, and nobody else seemed to have noticed it. I take it and see. It is a black notebook, very old.

I open the notebook. There are many word inside but I cannot understand, maybe it is a secret. I am very scare. I think maybe it is belong to a bad guy. I want to give it to police but the minibus is going very fast and I am late for school.

When I arrive school, I show the notebook to my best friend Tom. Tom say we should keep it and find the treasure. We are very excited. After school we go to the place in the notebook. It is a old building in Mong Kok. There are many people and very noisy. We find a door, we open the door. Suddenly a man shout at us. We are very scared and run away very fast.

Then I wake up. It is only a dream. My mother call me to wake up and go to school. I feel very relief. I think we should not take other people thing. If we find something, we should give to police. It is the correct thing to do. This is my story. I hope you like it.

commentary.content: The given sentence is used, but the plot is thin and confused: the notebook suddenly leads to treasure with no explanation, the events in Mong Kok are not developed, and the 'only a dream' ending cancels the story. It finishes with a moral and an appeal to the reader.
commentary.language: Tense switches to the present after the first sentence and errors are frequent in agreement and word form (I am very scare; Tom say; a man shout at us). Vocabulary is very limited.
commentary.organisation: Events are in sequence and paragraphs are recognisable, but connections are weak (find the treasure appears from nowhere) and the ending is abrupt.
